name: Lying about height / dating app height
lead: Listing a taller height than one's measured height on a dating app, sometimes called height padding or height inflation, is a practice discussed in looksmaxxing and dating communities as a way to appear taller to potential partners. Apps ask for a height and some let users filter by it, so the number entered can determine whether a profile appears in a search or is passed over at a glance.

Proponents on looksmax.org describe it as common behavior: one poster claims that people in daily life state heights one to two inches above their real height and that celebrities state two to three inches more [1]. Others on the forum argue that stated heights are inflated across the board and that listed numbers should be read accordingly [2][3].

General research finds that people tend to report being taller than they measure, with the gap varying by height, age, sex and region [4]. Studies of partner preference have reported that many women favor taller male partners and that shorter men are rated less favorably on average [5]. No published study has measured height inflation on dating apps or the outcomes for people who list a taller height.

angle.text: People who list a taller height do so to pass height filters and to be read as taller in the first stage of dating. It changes the stated number rather than the person's actual stature, so it is often discussed together with shoes and lifts that add real height in person.

paras: Dating apps typically ask users to enter a height, and some allow filtering by it. Community discussions describe entering a figure a few centimeters or an inch or more above one's true height, sometimes rounding up to a threshold such as six feet. Because the practice is private and unverifiable, there is no reliable figure for how common it is among dating-app users.

A looksmax.org thread argues that height inflation is about people claiming a height they do not have, and that stating about two inches more online and in conversation is typical; the poster pairs this with thick-soled shoes and insoles that add real height in person [1]. Another thread lists how heights are perceived, with entries such as 5'9" being the new 5'7", reflecting a belief that listed heights have drifted upward [2]. Users also post screenshots of people reacting to heights like 6'2" as not tall, and suggest that someone shorter told them a taller number [3]. Other threads discuss why inflation seems worse than it is and male height inflation more broadly [6][7].

A general reference work on human height notes that self-reported height tends to exceed measured height, and that the discrepancy differs by height, age, gender and region [4]. This is a finding about surveys and records in general, not specifically about dating profiles.

Sociological writing on height discrimination (heightism, a term coined in 1971) summarizes studies in which women's stated preferences favored taller partners, and in which shorter men were rated less favorably than average-height and tall men. One study found little difference in attractiveness between average-height and tall men. The same source notes that the height-attractiveness link reflects modern cultural norms rather than a universal trait; a study of Hadza foragers found height did not feature in mate choice, and a 2019 Hungarian survey found most respondents chose moderately tall ideal heights [5].
No studies found. Related research exists on height and partner preferences in general [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, height inflation is discussed both as something others do and as a tactic, alongside height lifts and shoes.

claims.claim: People routinely claim one to two inches more than their real height
claims.believers: A poster says people in real life claim 1-2 inches more and celebrities 2-3 inches more than their true height [1].
claims.experts: General survey research finds self-reported height tends to exceed measured height, with the gap varying by height, age and sex [4]. No study has measured it on dating apps.

claims.claim: Taller listed height improves dating outcomes
claims.believers: Forum users argue that listed height determines filtering and first impressions, so stating more is advantageous [1][2].
claims.experts: Studies summarized in the heightism literature report that many women favor taller men and rate shorter men less favorably on average, while noting this reflects cultural norms and is not universal [5]. No trial has tested outcomes of listing a taller height.

card.summary: Stating a taller height on a dating profile than you measure; common talk, almost no direct research.
card.note: No studies on dating-app outcomes of stating a taller height were found.

quick.overview:
Lying about height means listing a taller height than one's real one on a dating app or profile. Communities that believe height strongly affects dating discuss it as a workaround.

General research shows people tend to over-report height in surveys, and studies report that many women prefer taller men. No study of how inflated heights affect dating-app results was found.
quick.mechanism: Users enter a larger number in the profile height field or round up to a threshold height. Nothing verifies the figure until people meet.
quick.risks: Documented consequences are not studied. Discussions describe discovery at in-person meetings as the main risk. Dating apps' terms of service generally address misleading profile information.
